title: q-Analog Geometric Series: Quantum Integers
description: A self-contained Lean development of the quantum integer [n]_q = 1 + q + … + q^{n-1} (the truncated geometric series), with its four structural laws: the geometric closed form, the classical limit [n]_1 = n, the additive cocycle law [m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m·[n]_q, and the multiplicative base-change law [m·n]_q = [m]_{q^n}·[n]_q. Mathlib has the geometric sum but no named q-integer theory.

originalContributions: Definition of the quantum integer qNat q n = ∑_{i<n} q^i over an arbitrary commutative ring (a q-integer structure Mathlib does not name)
Additive cocycle law qNat_add: [m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m·[n]_q, proved by induction — the q-deformation of m+n
Multiplicative base-change law qNat_mul: [m·n]_q = [m]_{q^n}·[n]_q, with the base change q ↦ q^n that has no q=1 shadow, proved by induction from the additive law
Geometric closed form qNat_mul_qSub (any comm ring) and the field quotient form qNat_eq_div for q ≠ 1, packaged for the q-integer

overview.historicalContext: The quantum integer (or q-integer) $[n]_q = 1 + q + q^2 + \cdots + q^{n-1}$ is the q-analog of the natural number $n$. As $q \to 1$ each term tends to $1$, so $[n]_1 = n$ and the q-integer degenerates to the ordinary integer. q-integers are the atoms of q-calculus: the q-factorial $[n]_q! = [1]_q[2]_q\cdots[n]_q$ and the Gaussian (q-binomial) coefficients $\binom{n}{k}_q$ are built from them. They count subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, index the representation theory of quantum groups, and organize the theory of integer partitions (the Rogers–Ramanujan identities live here). The standard reference is Kac and Cheung, *Quantum Calculus* (Springer, 2002).
overview.problemStatement:
Define the **quantum integer** over a commutative ring $R$ with parameter $q \in R$ as the truncated geometric series
$$[n]_q := \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i = 1 + q + q^2 + \cdots + q^{n-1}.$$
Establish its defining structural laws: (1) the geometric closed form $[n]_q(q-1) = q^n - 1$; (2) the classical limit $[n]_1 = n$; (3) the additive law $[m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m[n]_q$; (4) the multiplicative law $[mn]_q = [m]_{q^n}[n]_q$.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Geometric closed form** $[n]_q(q-1) = q^n-1$ is Mathlib's `geom_sum_mul` applied to the definition; over a field with $q \neq 1$ it rearranges to $[n]_q = (q^n-1)/(q-1)$ via `geom_sum_eq`.

**Index recurrence** $[n+1]_q = [n]_q + q^n$ follows from `Finset.sum_range_succ` and is the workhorse for the inductions below.

**Additive law** is proved by induction on $n$. The successor step writes $m+(n+1) = (m+n)+1$, applies the recurrence on both sides, and closes by `ring` after expanding $q^{m+n} = q^m q^n$.

**Multiplicative law** is proved by induction on $m$. Writing $(m{+}1)n = mn + n$, the additive law splits $[mn+n]_q = [mn]_q + q^{mn}[n]_q$; the inductive hypothesis rewrites $[mn]_q = [m]_{q^n}[n]_q$, and the recurrence in base $q^n$ gives $[m{+}1]_{q^n} = [m]_{q^n} + (q^n)^m$. The two sides match once $(q^n)^m = q^{mn}$ (by `pow_mul` and commutativity of $\mathbb{N}$ multiplication).
keyInsights: **The q-integer is literally a geometric series.** $[n]_q = \sum_{i<n} q^i$, so Mathlib's generic `geom_sum` lemmas supply the closed form for free — the q-analog content is in the *combinatorial* laws, not the closed form.

**The additive cocycle factor $q^m$ is the whole point.** $[m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m[n]_q$ rather than $[m]_q + [n]_q$: the shift by $q^m$ is exactly what makes the q-integers a non-trivial deformation of $\mathbb{N}$, and it is the source of the $q$-counting in Gaussian binomials.

**The multiplicative law changes the base.** $[mn]_q = [m]_{q^n}[n]_q$ — the first factor is evaluated at $q^n$, not $q$. At $q=1$ the identity collapses to $mn = m\cdot n$ and the base change becomes invisible, so this is a genuinely q-flavoured fact with no classical shadow.

**Everything reduces to one recurrence.** Both structural inductions run on $[n+1]_q = [n]_q + q^n$; the additive law then bootstraps the multiplicative law, so the entire theory rests on a single `Finset.sum_range_succ` rewrite.

**Mathlib gap.** Mathlib formalizes the geometric sum but has no named quantum integer, q-factorial, or Gaussian-binomial; this entry supplies the q-integer layer and its laws as a reusable, 0-axiom foundation.

sections.title: The quantum integer
sections.summary: Defines qNat q n = ∑_{i<n} q^i over a commutative ring, with the base cases [0]_q = 0, [1]_q = 1 and the index recurrence [n+1]_q = [n]_q + q^n.
sections.mathContext: The q-integer as a truncated geometric series; the recurrence is the engine for all later inductions.

sections.title: Geometric closed form
sections.summary: qNat_mul_qSub: [n]_q·(q-1) = q^n-1 in any commutative ring, and qNat_at_one: [n]_1 = n.
sections.mathContext: Connects the q-integer to Mathlib's geom_sum_mul and records the classical limit q → 1.

sections.title: Additive law
sections.summary: qNat_add: [m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m·[n]_q, by induction on n.
sections.mathContext: The q-analog of addition; the cocycle factor q^m is the structural heart of q-calculus.

sections.title: Multiplicative law
sections.summary: qNat_mul: [m·n]_q = [m]_{q^n}·[n]_q, by induction on m using the additive law.
sections.mathContext: The q-analog of multiplication, with a base change q ↦ q^n invisible at q = 1.

sections.title: Field quotient form
sections.summary: qNat_eq_div: over a field with q ≠ 1, [n]_q = (q^n-1)/(q-1).
sections.mathContext: The familiar division formula, valid once division is available and q ≠ 1.

conclusion.summary: Starting from the single definition [n]_q = ∑_{i<n} q^i, this entry proves the four laws that characterize the quantum integer: the geometric closed form, the classical limit [n]_1 = n, the additive cocycle law [m+n]_q = [m]_q + q^m[n]_q, and the multiplicative base-change law [mn]_q = [m]_{q^n}[n]_q. All are fully machine-checked with 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: These laws are the foundation on which q-factorials and Gaussian binomial coefficients are built. The additive cocycle and multiplicative base-change identities are precisely the q-analog facts that Mathlib's generic geometric-sum lemmas do not package, so this entry is a reusable starting point for further q-calculus formalization in the gallery.
openQuestions: Build the q-factorial [n]_q! = ∏_{k=1}^n [k]_q and the Gaussian binomial coefficient on top of qNat, then prove the q-Pascal recurrence and the q-binomial theorem (Gauss).
Prove the q-analog of unique-factorization-style statements, e.g. that [n]_q ∣ [m]_q in ℤ[q] iff n ∣ m, linking q-integers to cyclotomic polynomials.
Establish the partition-theoretic interpretation: the Gaussian binomial counts lattice paths / subspaces of 𝔽_q^n, giving a combinatorial proof of the q-binomial theorem.

crossReferences.description: The base geometric series formula (Wiedijk #66). The quantum integer is its truncated, parametric form [n]_q = ∑_{i<n} q^i.
Another q/geometric-series extension: the Euler product expresses ζ(s) as a product of (infinite) geometric series, where this entry develops the finite q-integer truncation.
